The following exhibits are series of traffic counts performed by the Virginia Department of Highways in October, 1971, and the Bureau of Traffic Engineering of the City of Richmond in December, 1971. All these locations lie within the boundaries of the Randolph Urban Renewal Area. The Bureau of Traffic Engineering representative who compiles all the relatively current data available stated that the Bureau estimates the annual average increase in traffic for Richmond city streets to be 3%. However, he added that it's a likely possibility that traffic in the Randolph area has not increased at that high a rate. Although we have contacted the recommended information source, there appears to be no predicted traffic data available to HUD for future vehicular movement in Randolph except for the Downtown Expressway.
The traffic count data supplied indicates that even though there is moderately heavy traffic on certain streets in Randolph, the completion of the Expressway will sharply increase the traffic moving through the northern portion of the project area. At the time of the traffic counts and at the present time, Idlewood Avenue has been one of the more heavily travelled east-west streets in Randolph. Other east-west streets in the community would not be expected to have significantly greater levels of traffic than the 24 hour 2-way traffic total of 6929 recorded at Location No. 6 on Idlewood. Given a 3% increase in each of the interim years since the counts were undertaken the 1973 updated figure would still only be 7351 vehicles. And assuming that the 3% annual increase remains valid in the future, the 1985 predicted traffic count over a 24hour period would be 10,481. This number shows a marked contrast with 1985 average traffic volume projection on the expressway, estimated at some 56,000 vehicles. The very substantial differentation before and after the arterial construction documents the Statement's contention that 'The Downtown Expressway will . . . greatly increase the number of automobiles passing through the Randolph Project".

' This opinion should be deleted unless it can be documented by 'before' as well as 'after' air quality analyses. Refer to Question 1 in the HUD response to the Environmental Protection Agency's comments.
4. "In Chapter III, paragraph A-1, on page 38, the inference is made that if the Randolph project is not implemented, then the Downtown Expressway would (upon construction) contribute to continuing problems and deterioration." This statement indicates a misinterpretation of this section. The paragraph under discussion was explaining the consequences of a "no action" alternative. Given the alternative the impacts of the Expressway, whether positive, negative, or neutral, would continue to affect the primarily residential community that Randolph is now.
